bibl.title: Animal Metacognition: A Tale of Two Comparative Psychologies

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The associative models offered to explain animals' uncertainty responses, and what adopting them costs comparative psychology theoretically.
span.quote: The authors summarize the empirical and theoretical situation regarding these associative descriptions.

span.label: critique
span.quote: The associative descriptions in the animal-metacognition literature fail to encompass important phenomena.

span.label: animal metacognition (uncertainty monitoring)
span.quote: A growing literature considers whether animals have capacities that are akin to human metacognition (i. e., humans’ capacity to monitor their states of uncertainty and knowing).

span.label: review
span.quote: The present article summarizes the empirical and theoretical situation regarding these associative models and descriptions of animal-metacognition phenomena.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: When deferred feedback camouflages the task's reinforcement structure, the animal builds its own subjective decisional framework and responds uncertain to whatever is near its own subjective breakpoint, not the task's objective one
span.quote: Absent access to the task’s associative structure, the animal constructed his own subjective decisional framework based on subjective difficulty, or uncertainty, or even metacognition.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Uncertainty responses draw on executive attention and working memory, which is why occupying those resources with a concurrent task selectively degrades them while leaving stimulus-driven perceptual classification intact
span.quote: This dissociation suggests that the uncertainty response is a higher-level, decisional response that is particularly dependent on working memory and attentional resources.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In Hampton's task no memory-relevant stimulus is present at choice time, so the animal must itself initiate and restrict a search of memory for a strong trace — an operation with no associative cue to react to
span.quote: What the animal must do is use those response icons to cue a memory search for a hot or recent trace.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Casting every performance as a register of activation strengths updated by reinforcement artificially equates psychologically different performances, which is what empties the label 'associative' of content
span.quote: Indeed, forcing all performances onto this structure artificially equates them—really, this is what you want to do and what you have to do if you want to label them all associative.

span.label: The uncertainty response is designed to carry no reward of its own, so choosing it cannot be explained by direct reinforcement of that response
span.quote: It would never bring any direct reward or other consequence.

span.label: In the memory task the response icons carry no trace-strength information, so there is nothing on the screen for an association to attach to - the animal must initiate its own search
span.quote: In this case, there are no memory-relevant stimuli on the scene. There is nothing to cue the animal’s response to some stimulus’s trace hotness.

span.label: The search must also be restricted to the right memory locations, and nothing in the display can tell the animal how to do that
span.quote: And nothing on the response screen can cue the macaque associatively to conduct this search of memory or to restrict that search to the required set of memory locations, or on how to judge when a remembered item has been retrieved or has not been retrieved.

span.label: The associative models work by mapping every performance onto one abstract register of activations updated by reinforcement, which is precisely what makes them unable to tell performances apart
span.quote: Indeed, forcing all performances onto this structure artificially equates them—really, this is what you want to do and what you have to do if you want to label them all associative.

span.label: The reductio: the same formalism works with a register of fully conscious metacognitive states updated by reinforcement, which shows the formalism settles nothing
span.quote: In this way, we could claim mathematically and formally that animals learn associatively through reinforcement to use fully conscious metacognitive states. This claim is useless.

span.label: The all-or-none framing is itself the error: uncertainty monitoring may exist in graded stages without the whole human package
span.quote: It can acknowledge that a capacity like metacognition may not be all or none, and that animals might have a basic uncertainty-monitoring system without having bought all the apps of human metacognition, like consciousness, self-awareness, and even self-loathing from cognitive failure and indecision.

span.label: The authors concede that not all of the models they criticise have had a fair opportunity to address the newest phenomenon.
span.quote: There has not been time to address it yet.

span.label: They hedge their own positive interpretation: information-seeking need not imply full conscious metacognition.
span.quote: Of course one need not attribute full, conscious, self-imbued metacognition to macaques even if one adopts this information-seeking hypothesis.

span.label: They acknowledge they cannot presently settle whether one criticised model succeeds in practice.
span.quote: It is presently difficult to judge the model’s pragmatic success.

span.label: The empirical results themselves are not in dispute - the whole disagreement is over interpretation
span.quote: These empirical results are not disputed.

span.label: The animals report nothing, so the human evidence for conscious uncertainty has no counterpart in the animal case
span.quote: Macaques have also shown this pattern repeatedly, though they report nothing.

span.label: The paper's own positive claim is hedged to possibly-metacognitive rather than metacognitive
span.quote: The research clearly suggests that what animals do in some tasks is higher-level and cognitive, deliberate and decisional, and possibly metacognitive and conscious.

span.label: The critique is of a specific class of models, which the authors accept would be a legitimate goal if it could be made to work
span.quote: As part of this consideration, some associative modelers have attempted to describe animals’ “metacognitive” performances in low-level, associative terms—an important goal if achievable.

span.label: associative - the specific sense: responding cued by a present stimulus or trained by reinforcement contingencies
span.quote: That is, those performances might have low-level and non-metacognitive bases if animals’ uncertainty responses were really cued by stimuli or conditioned/trained by reinforcement contingencies.

span.label: associative - the stretched sense: anything expressible as a register of activations updated by reward, which covers everything and therefore distinguishes nothing
span.quote: Unfortunately, then the associative label becomes meaningless, because one can no longer make distinctions among performances that may be highly distinctive theoretically and psychologically.

span.label: the task - with trace-relevant stimuli present (matching-to-sample): an associative account applies
span.quote: In these tasks, there are stimuli on the scene at the moment of behavioral choice that are memory or trace-strength relevant.

span.label: the task - with memory-neutral response icons (Hampton): nothing is present to be associated with, so the same account does not carry over
span.quote: However, Hampton’s methodology is strikingly different. His macaques, after observing the sample and waiting through the retention interval, are presented with two abstract response icons that have no trace-strength relevance.

span.label: metacognition - as all-or-none: the Yes/No framing the paper says the dichotomy itself may be wrong for the field's goal
span.quote: Even in Le Pelley’s (2012) title—Metacognitive Monkeys or Associative Animals…—he seems to recommend a Yes or No answer to the question of animal metacognition, when that dichotomy could be wrong for the field’s theoretical goal.

span.label: metacognition - as graded: a basic uncertainty-monitoring system without consciousness or self-awareness attached
span.quote: It can acknowledge that a capacity like metacognition may not be all or none, and that animals might have a basic uncertainty-monitoring system without having bought all the apps of human metacognition, like consciousness, self-awareness, and even self-loathing from cognitive failure and indecision.

span.label: contradicts → Le Pelley (2012), associative-learning model of animal metacognition
span.quote: This poor fit by itself sharply undermines the descriptive value of Le Pelley’s associative-learning model in this case.

span.label: contradicts → Jozefowiez et al. (2009a)
span.quote: For the same reason, Jozefowiez et al. (2009a) are incorrect when they claim that the underlying processes are exactly the same whether a triggering stimulus is on the screen or the animal must initiate its own targeted search for active memory traces.

span.label: builds-on → Hampton (2001), macaque metamemory studies
span.quote: The results in Smith et al. (in press) also offer a new perspective on Hampton’s (2001) metamemory studies.

span.label: critiques → associative models of animal uncertainty responses (Jozefowiez et al., Le Pelley, Staddon et al.)
span.quote: For the same reason, Jozefowiez et al. (2009a) are incorrect when they claim that the underlying processes are exactly the same whether a triggering stimulus is on the screen or the animal must initiate its own targeted search for active memory traces.

span.label: critiques → strict application of Morgan's canon in comparative psychology
span.quote: Those models reflect an ultimately strict adherence to Morgan’s (1906) Canon, which even Morgan did not intend and which many comparative-cognition researchers do not accept now.

span.label: supports → Hampton (2001) and the memory-monitoring evidence for macaque metacognition
span.quote: Therefore, viewed from all these perspectives, the performances observed in Hampton (2001) cannot properly be considered to be based on associative learning, and overlooking this point is a significant error.

span.label: supports → Metcalfe's operational benchmark of stimulus absence
span.quote: Moreover, Metcalfe (2008) made stimulus absence in metacognitive tasks a crucial benchmark in her operational definition of animal metacognition.

span.label: uncertainty response —operationalised-as→ uncertainty monitoring
span.quote: They would also be given an “uncertainty response” (UR) with which to decline to complete any trials they choose.

span.label: associative —contrasted-with→ metacognition
span.quote: They insist on a qualitative distinction between metacognitive and associative performances, when, of course, there could be levels and gradations between, involving executive function, attentional resources, and so forth as precursors to full awareness and declarative cognition.

span.label: registers —operationalised-as→ associative
span.quote: They offer a universalist definition of associative learning (the registers, the reinforcements, the updatings), and a universalist null hypothesis claiming that animals’ uncertainty performances can be explained in purely associative ways.

span.label: trace strength —part-of→ Delayed-Matching-to-Sample
span.quote: In these tasks, there are stimuli on the scene at the moment of behavioral choice that are memory or trace-strength relevant.

span.label: executive —causes→ uncertainty response
span.quote: The concurrent memory-load results of Smith et al. (in press) further suggest that the processes that support URs in monitoring tasks are executive and attentional, not automatic and reactive.

span.label: operational definition —operationalised-as→ metacognition
span.quote: Moreover, Metcalfe (2008) made stimulus absence in metacognitive tasks a crucial benchmark in her operational definition of animal metacognition.

span.label: Morgan —causes→ associative
span.quote: Those models reflect an ultimately strict adherence to Morgan’s (1906) Canon, which even Morgan did not intend and which many comparative-cognition researchers do not accept now.

span.label: metacognition —part-of→ declarative
span.quote: It is linked to their declarative cognitive system ( Nelson, 1996 ; Koriat, 2007 ) and self-awareness ( Gallup, 1982 ).

span.label: self-awareness —distinct-from→ uncertainty monitoring
span.quote: It can acknowledge that a capacity like metacognition may not be all or none, and that animals might have a basic uncertainty-monitoring system without having bought all the apps of human metacognition, like consciousness, self-awareness, and even self-loathing from cognitive failure and indecision.

span.label: reinforcement —causes→ registers
span.quote: The registers are updated based on the rewards and penalties for correct and incorrect responses, so that the register’s activations reflect the reinforcement history in the task.

span.label: phylogenetic —causes→ metacognition
span.quote: It ignores that phylogeny probably gave reflective mind and metacognition to animals in stages of attainment, so that the stages of the emergence from monkeys to apes to humans could be crucial in understanding the rise of our reflective mind.

span.label: macaques —part-of→ uncertainty response
span.quote: Macaques have also shown this pattern repeatedly, though they report nothing.

span.label: chimpanzees —part-of→ uncertainty monitoring
span.quote: Thus, chimpanzees showed efficient information-seeking behavior that suggested they knew whether they knew the item’s identity when it was time to name it (see also Call, 2010 ; Call & Carpenter, 2001 ).

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Figure 1D shows generally that there was a strong relationship between the proportion of trials declined and the decisional distance of the trial level from the animal’s decisional breakpoint ( r = 0.838).

span.label: goodness-of-fit measure
span.quote: To summarize the fits, we used the Average Absolute Deviation (AAD) that represents the average of the 120 errors of prediction, with all errors of prediction taken positively.

span.label: model fitting
span.quote: We also fit these runs of the model to Smith et al.’s (2006) data.

span.label: signal detection theory model
span.quote: For example, Smith et al. (2008) developed an associative model based in signal-detection theory.

span.label: error of prediction
span.quote: The error of prediction between predicted and observed response proportions was 5%, and this is large in almost all formal-analytic domains (e.g., Smith et al., in press ; Smith, Redford, & Haas, 2008 ).

span.label: Re-running Le Pelley's associative-learning model shows it can only shift the uncertainty-response curve leftward by making the uncertainty response dominate the whole stimulus range, so it never reproduces the macaque's actual pattern.
span.quote: Consequently, Le Pelley’s model never produces anything like the UR data pattern that Smith et al. observed ( Figure 1C ).

span.label: At its best fit the associative model mispredicts each of 120 data points by .10 on average.
span.quote: The associative model at best (i.e., at the minimum AAD) averaged a misprediction of .10 for each of 120 data points.

span.label: A non-associative uncertainty model fits the same data more than three times more closely, with an AAD of .03.
span.quote: The AAD for that model fit to the same data is only .03, a far closer fit than achieved by the associative-learning model.

span.label: The better-fitting cognitive model is also the more parsimonious one, using 3 free parameters against the associative model's 5.
span.quote: Not only that, but the cognitive model needs only 3 parameters to fit the data, not the 5 that Le Pelley uses.

span.label: The associative model achieves its best fit precisely by predicting a symmetric uncertainty curve centred on the task's true breakpoint, i.e. by abandoning the displaced Level-14 centring that is the result needing explanation.
span.quote: Thus, the model fits best when it simply gives up predicting the crucial result that the macaque showed: an asymmetrical centering of the UR at Level 14, in sharp disalignment with the task’s associative structure.

span.label: Capuchin monkeys almost never used the uncertainty response despite receiving immediate trial-by-trial feedback, which is the condition most favourable to associative learning.
span.quote: Strikingly, capuchin monkeys essentially did not use the UR ( Figure 3A ), even though in this experiment the capuchin monkeys received immediate feedback following every trial.

span.label: The same capuchins learned the Middle response to the same intermediate stimuli easily, so their failure was specific to the uncertainty response and cannot be an associative-learning deficit.
span.quote: The Sparse-Uncertain-Dense task, on the associative hypothesis, should have let capuchin monkeys associate URs to difficult discriminative stimuli.

span.label: A concurrent memory load selectively suppressed macaques' uncertainty responses while leaving their Sparse, Middle and Dense perceptual responses largely intact.
span.quote: Concurrent tasks disrupted macaques’ URs far more than their Sparse, Middle, or Dense perceptual responses.

span.label: Pigeons, which are excellent associative learners, show no memory-monitoring capacity in the paradigms where macaques do.
span.quote: They confirmed that pigeons do not express any memory-monitoring capacity.

span.label: Pigeons' uncertainty-response rate stays flat across retention intervals and they gain nothing from choosing which memory tests to take.
span.quote: Their UR curve stays flat over the range of retention intervals—they do not make more URs when given longer to forget (though they should because they remember less after longer delays).

span.label: To reproduce the serial-position results the associative model would need nine free parameters, a level of flexibility the authors say they have never seen accepted as plausible.
span.quote: Notice also that on adding these parameters the associative model in Le Pelley’s case would have nine free parameters (i.e., response variation, memory variation for foils, memory variation for samples, the primacy parameter, the recency parameter, reward value for errors, reward values for corrects, reward values for bailouts, and a scaling parameter).

span.label: Le Pelley's simulation of Hampton's task set the uncertainty response's reward value to zero although Hampton always rewarded it with a food pellet, so the published simulations misdescribe the method they claim to model.
span.quote: Nonetheless, the published simulations must be discounted because they misstate a crucial aspect of Hampton’s methodology.

span.label: Hampton's blank-trial control shows macaques were reading memory-trace strength rather than the length of the retention interval, since with delay held constant they declined blank trials far more often.
span.quote: Now, with delay interval controlled, animals made far more URs on blank trials.

span.label: A single memory-monitoring model fitted to two separate studies recovers the same criterion of memory strength in both, a convergence the associative models cannot produce.
span.quote: They found that monkeys defended the same criterion of memory strength in both studies, a striking convergence across laboratories, animals, and methodologies.

span.label: The authors argue that a strict associative reading of comparative data exaggerates the distance between human and animal minds and strips animal models of value for studying human metacognition.
span.quote: Those models reflect an ultimately strict adherence to Morgan’s (1906) Canon, which even Morgan did not intend and which many comparative-cognition researchers do not accept now.

span.label: animals show uncertainty responses where no cuing stimulus is present, on first trials, and without feedback
span.quote: They can respond uncertain absent any cuing stimuli ( Hampton, 2001 ), on the first trial of novel tasks ( Washburn, Smith, & Shields, 2006 ), and even when there are no immediate feedback or reinforcement signals so that the processes of conditioning and association are ruled out ( Smith, Beran, Redford, & Washburn, 2006 ).

span.label: chimpanzees checked the container before naming only on trials where they had not seen its contents
span.quote: Chimpanzees were significantly more likely to visit the food container first—before choosing a lexigram—on trials in which they did not know the container’s contents.

span.label: the empirical pattern is agreed by both sides; only its interpretation is disputed
span.quote: These empirical results are not disputed.

span.label: a broad enough associative label can no longer separate performances that differ psychologically
span.quote: Unfortunately, then the associative label becomes meaningless, because one can no longer make distinctions among performances that may be highly distinctive theoretically and psychologically.

span.label: the same formal machinery can model fully conscious metacognitive states, so the formalism decides nothing
span.quote: Moreover, this claim implies that any kind of information processing can be lumped under the construct associative, which makes that term theoretically useless.

span.label: metacognition
span.quote: Metacognition is the capacity to monitor and control one’s cognitive processes.

span.label: uncertainty response (UR)
span.quote: They would also be given an “uncertainty response” (UR) with which to decline to complete any trials they choose.

span.label: Middle response (MR)
span.quote: By this interpretation, the UR would really just be a “Middle” response (MR), entrained just as Sparse and Dense responses are, subject to reinforcement pressures and low-level associative-learning mechanisms just as Sparse and Dense responses are.

span.label: Average Absolute Deviation (AAD)
span.quote: To summarize the fits, we used the Average Absolute Deviation (AAD) that represents the average of the 120 errors of prediction, with all errors of prediction taken positively.

span.label: fulcrum point of URs
span.quote: This fulcrum point is the median trial level of URs—that is, the density level at which half the simulated observer’s URs lay above that level and half below that level.

span.label: subjective difficulty
span.quote: Subjective difficulty is non-associative because it is independent from reward, punishment, or reinforcement history.

span.label: uncertainty response
span.quote: They would also be given an “uncertainty response” (UR) with which to decline to complete any trials they choose.

span.label: Delayed-Matching-to-Sample
span.quote: in which animals see a sample picture, and then, after a retention interval, see a set of choice stimuli

span.label: feedback timing (trial-by-trial versus deferred over four trials)
span.term: feedback timing (trial-by-trial versus deferred over four trials)
span.quote: To test these descriptions, Smith et al. (2006 , also Couchman et al., 2010 ) replaced trial-by-trial feedback with deferred feedback whereby macaques worked for four trials before receiving any feedback.

span.label: concurrent working-memory load
span.quote: A requirement to perform concurrent memory tasks was occasionally added to ongoing perceptual-discrimination performance.

span.label: length of the penalty timeout
span.quote: They more than quadrupled the penalty timeout to 90 s from 20s.

span.label: retention interval (delay between sample and test)
span.term: retention interval (delay between sample and test)
span.quote: Now, with delay interval controlled, animals made far more URs on blank trials.

span.label: rate of uncertainty responses (trials declined)
span.quote: Concurrent tasks disrupted macaques’ URs far more than their Sparse, Middle, or Dense perceptual responses.

span.label: r = 0.838 — correlation between the proportion of trials the macaque declined and the distance of the trial level from his own subjective decisional breakpoint
span.quote: Figure 1D shows generally that there was a strong relationship between the proportion of trials declined and the decisional distance of the trial level from the animal’s decisional breakpoint ( r = 0.838).

span.label: .10 — best-case average absolute deviation of the associative-learning model per data point
span.quote: The associative model at best (i.e., at the minimum AAD) averaged a misprediction of .10 for each of 120 data points.

span.label: .03 — average absolute deviation of the non-associative uncertainty model on the same data
span.quote: The AAD for that model fit to the same data is only .03, a far closer fit than achieved by the associative-learning model.

span.label: about .30 — per-data-point error of the associative model when constrained to the UR fulcrum of 14 that the real macaque showed
span.quote: At a UR fulcrum of 14, shown by the real macaque, Le Pelley’s (2012) associative model would miss the real data by about .30 per data point—an extremely poor fit.

span.label: 5% — error of prediction of the earlier signal-detection associative model between predicted and observed response proportions
span.quote: The error of prediction between predicted and observed response proportions was 5%, and this is large in almost all formal-analytic domains (e.g., Smith et al., in press ; Smith, Redford, & Haas, 2008 ).

span.label: 7% — average per-stimulus-level misprediction of the uncertainty response by that associative model across levels 1-31
span.quote: From Levels 1–31, the theoretically important UR was mispredicted by 7% per stimulus level on average.

span.label: 23% ... 97% — macaque Murph's uncertainty-response rate at Level 9 against his accuracy on those same trials, showing URs uncoupled from reinforcement
span.quote: At Level 9, macaque Murph (in a Sparse-Dense discrimination task like that described in Section 1) made many URs (23%) for trials he answered 97% correct (when he tried them on other occasions).

span.label: 19% ... 22% — the same macaque's uncertainty-response rate at Level 20 against his accuracy there, far below chance yet declined less often than the easy level
span.quote: At Level 20, he made fewer URs (19%) for trials he answered 22% correct (when he tried them).

span.label: 14 and 0.12 — the real macaque's position in the simulation space (UR fulcrum, mean UR rate), which the associative model's runs never reach
span.quote: The real macaque’s performance point in this space is 14 and 0.12.

span.label: 90 s from 20s — the penalty timeout increase used to raise associative pressure on capuchins to adopt the uncertainty response
span.quote: They more than quadrupled the penalty timeout to 90 s from 20s.

span.label: five of six — capuchin monkeys who still failed to use the uncertainty response adaptively even after the timeout was quadrupled
span.quote: But still, five of six monkeys did not do so.

span.label: 10% — the constant error rate macaques maintained as memory lists lengthened, by declining more tests
span.quote: In addition, macaques held their error rate constant at 10% as the memory lists grew longer and the memory tests harder ( Figure 6B ).

span.label: one of five — capuchins who searched before reaching more often on unseen-hiding trials in the food-concealment paradigm
span.quote: In one capuchin experiment, only one of five capuchins searched before reaching more often on trials where the hiding event was unseen compared to when it was seen.

span.label: 41-step continuum — the density scale along which stimuli are classified sparse or dense
span.quote: For example, stimulus rectangles—to be classified as Sparse or Dense—might vary along a 41-step continuum in their density of lit pixels.

span.label: Level 21 — the exact breakpoint, never presented, around which the uncertainty response should cluster
span.quote: Levels 1–20 would be rewarded as Sparse; Levels 22–41 as Dense; Level 21—the exact breakpoint of the discrimination—would not be presented.
